summary: Defines an OSPF-based auto-discovery mechanism for Layer 1 VPNs, so provider edge devices learn about each other and about customer edge links and their VPN associations. It provides discovery for Basic Mode. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Provider routers need to find each other and see which customers connect where. This uses OSPF messages to share that information.

questions: what is opaque type 5 in ospf
how do pe routers discover l1vpn ports
what is the l1vpn info tlv
subtitle: How provider edge routers use OSPF to learn which customer links belong to which Layer 1 VPN.

tldr.problem: In a Layer 1 VPN, provider edge devices need to know which customer ports and provider ports map to each VPN, and that information could otherwise only be provisioned by hand.
tldr.mechanism: Each provider edge device floods a new type of OSPF Opaque LSA, the L1VPN LSA, for every local customer-to-provider link, carrying the VPN identifier, the PE TE address and the auto-discovery information.
tldr.outcome: In steady state every PE that serves a given L1VPN ends up with identical port tables for it. The RFC itself warns that flooding these LSAs to every router can raise scalability concerns in large networks.

today: RFC 5252 is a Proposed Standard from July 2008 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the OSPF route to L1VPN Basic Mode auto-discovery; the BGP alternative is in RFC 5195.

sections.title: Auto-Discovery for Layer 1 VPNs
sections.content:
RFC 5252 defines an auto-discovery mechanism for Layer 1 VPNs (L1VPNs) built on OSPF version 2. It builds on the L1VPN framework in RFC 4847 and the Basic Mode defined in RFC 5251. Basic Mode needs a mapping between customer port identifiers (CPI) and provider port identifiers (PPI), and says this mapping may come from provisioning or from auto-discovery. This RFC supplies the auto-discovery option.

The goal is that provider edge (PE) devices dynamically learn about each other, about the attributes of configured customer edge (CE) links and about the L1VPNs those links belong to. OSPF version 3 and IPv6 are out of scope and are to be defined separately.

A parallel mechanism that uses BGP exists in RFC 5195. The OSPF approach is described as particularly useful in networks where BGP is not typically used.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers plug into the edge of a big network. The edge routers need a way to find out who is plugged in where, without a person typing it into every machine.

sections.title: Roles and the Port Information Table
sections.content:
The RFC uses four kinds of network element. A CE is a customer device directly connected to the provider network. A PE is a provider device directly connected to one or more customer networks. A P is a provider core device that has no direct customer connections. A C is a customer device that is not connected to the provider network.

Each PE keeps a Port Information Table (PIT) for every L1VPN it serves. Entries in the PIT hold the <CPI, PPI> tuples that tie customer port identifiers to provider port identifiers. Auto-discovery is how those tables are filled in and kept current.
sections.plainLanguage: Each edge router keeps one address book per customer group. Each entry says which customer plug matches which plug on the provider side.

sections.title: The L1VPN LSA
sections.content:
Discovery information travels in a new Opaque LSA called the L1VPN LSA. Its header fields (LS age, Options, Advertising Router, LS Sequence Number, LS checksum and Length) are as defined in RFC 2328, and Opaque ID is as defined in RFC 5250.

Two fields are fixed by this RFC. LS Type MUST be 11, an AS-scoped Opaque LSA, and Opaque Type MUST be 5. The body carries TLVs: exactly one L1VPN Info TLV MUST be present (if more appear, only the first is processed and the others MUST be ignored), and a single TE Link TLV from RFC 3630 and RFC 4203 MAY be included.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a standard OSPF envelope with a special label on it, so routers that do not care about it know to pass it along without reading the contents.

sections.title: The L1VPN Info TLV
sections.content:
The L1VPN Info TLV (named L1VPN IPv4 Info, type 1, variable length) carries the actual discovery data. After a 4-byte TLV header it holds these fields:

  • L1VPN Globally Unique Identifier, as defined in RFC 5251.
  • PE TE Address, which MUST be an address the LSA originator advertised per RFC 3630, either the Router Address TLV or a Local interface IP address link sub-TLV. It will typically be the TE Router Address.
  • Link Local Identifier, which for an unnumbered PE TE link MUST hold the value advertised per RFC 4203, and for a numbered link MUST be 0.
  • L1VPN Auto-discovery information, as defined in RFC 5251.
  • Padding, only when the information is not 4-byte aligned. It MUST be less than 4 bytes and MUST NOT be present when the information is already aligned.

The TLV Length counts the TLV excluding its 4-byte header and any padding.
sections.plainLanguage: The special note says which customer group it is about, which provider router is talking, which plug it is, and the details of the match. Extra blank space is added at the end only to make the note line up neatly.

sections.title: Advertising and Processing
sections.content:
Each PE MUST originate a separate L1VPN LSA, with AS flooding scope, for each local CE-to-PE link. The LSA MUST be originated every time the PE restarts and every time the PIT entry for that link changes. It MUST include a single L1VPN Info TLV and MAY include a single TE Link TLV carrying the TE attributes of the CE-to-PE link. Those attributes are not advertised by normal OSPF-TE procedures because CEs are outside the provider TE domain. Extra TLVs SHOULD be ignored by receiving PEs.

Because the LSA is AS-scoped it is flooded to all PEs in the AS as described in RFC 5250. When a PE receives a new, removed or modified L1VPN LSA, it MUST check whether it keeps a PIT for the L1VPN named in the identifier field. If it does, it SHOULD add, remove or modify the matching PIT entry. An implementation MAY choose not to remove or modify entries, according to local policy or management directives. In the normal steady state all PEs for a given L1VPN have identical PITs.
sections.plainLanguage: Whenever a branch gets a new customer plug, or restarts, it announces it to everyone. Each branch that serves the same customer group updates its address book.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example has three PEs. PE1 connects CE11 and CE15 in L1VPN1 and CE22 in L1VPN2. PE2 connects CE13 in L1VPN1, and PE3 connects CE24 in L1VPN2. PE1 therefore keeps two PITs, while PE2 and PE3 keep one each.

PE1 originates three L1VPN LSAs, one each for the links PE1-CE11, PE1-CE22 and PE1-CE15. PE2 and PE3 each originate one. In steady state, PIT1 on PE1 and PE3 holds entries for PE1-CE11, PE1-CE15 and PE2-CE13, and PIT2 on PE1 and PE2 holds entries for PE1-CE22 and PE3-CE24. The P router has no L1VPN links, so it originates no LSAs and keeps no PITs, but it still floods and stores them.

The mechanism does not stop a PE from applying local policy to its PIT, for example permanent static entries or ignoring LSAs from a particular TE. The PE TE Address must match a valid PE TE Router ID or numbered TE Link ID so that CEs can be resolved to the PE as known to the Traffic Engineering Database and TE paths toward the CEs can be computed.
sections.plainLanguage: Three branches each shout about their own customers. At the end, every branch that works for a customer group knows about all of that group's plugs, even at the other branches.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Per RFC 5250, OSPF speakers that do not support L1VPN auto-discovery, such as P routers, simply take part in flooding the L1VPN LSAs and should ignore their contents, so the RFC finds no interoperability issues.

The scalability cost is stated openly: a P router that has no L1VPN links still holds every L1VPN LSA in its link state database, which the RFC calls a cause for scalability concerns that could prove problematic in large networks.

On security, delivering VPN membership information to CEs is out of scope, so the issues are limited to the OSPF domain. The approach reuses RFC 2328 and RFC 5250, so the same OSPF protections apply, including several types of authentication, limits on how often LSAs are originated and accepted, and techniques to limit database overflow. For end-to-end authentication, the experimental extension in RFC 2154 supports signing and authenticating LSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers that do not know about this feature just pass the notes along unread. The downside is that they still have to store every note, which could get heavy in a very large network.

fields.name: L1VPN TLV Length
fields.desc: Length excluding the 4-byte header and any padding.

fields.name: L1VPN Globally Unique Identifier
fields.desc: Identifies the L1VPN, as defined in RFC 5251.

fields.name: PE TE Address
fields.desc: Address advertised by the LSA originator per RFC 3630.

fields.name: Link Local Identifier
fields.desc: Identifier for unnumbered links; 0 for numbered links.
